description: Inositol phosphate signalling is not confined to the cytoplasm: the nucleus maintains its own pool of inositol trisphosphate and tetrakisphosphate, which feed nuclear kinases and phosphatases and influence chromatin regulation, mRNA export and calcium release from nuclear envelope stores. Movement of IP3 and IP4 between cytosol and nucleoplasm supplies that pool, and it occurs across the nuclear pore complex, whose scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins are represented here alongside the Y-complex components, the central channel proteins, the basket formed by TPR and NUP153, and cytoplasmic filament elements such as RANBP2 and NUP214. Whether these small, highly charged metabolites simply diffuse through the pore's permeability barrier or are carried by a dedicated transporter is unresolved. Pore integrity therefore sets the boundary conditions for nuclear inositol phosphate signalling, and nucleoporin defects disturb nucleocytoplasmic exchange broadly, as in triple A syndrome caused by loss of AAAS.

Parasympathetic input to the pancreas amplifies insulin release during a meal, and this cholinergic arm explains why insulin output is larger when food is anticipated and ingested than when the same glucose load is given intravenously. The potentiation is conditional on glucose already being elevated, so the nerve signal boosts rather than initiates secretion, and loss of this vagal control blunts the early phase of the insulin response. Acetylcholine acts on the M3 muscarinic receptor of beta cells, which couples through Gq-family alpha subunits to phospholipase C beta. Hydrolysis of PIP2 yields IP3, releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores to drive granule exocytosis, and diacylglycerol, which recruits and activates protein kinase C alpha at the membrane. PKC alpha phosphorylates MARCKS, an actin- and membrane-binding substrate linked to granule trafficking and the mobilisation of insulin vesicles for release.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase makes the nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, restrains platelet adhesion and leukocyte recruitment, and sets basal blood pressure; losing its output is a defining feature of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, atherosclerosis and diabetes. eNOS activation describes how the enzyme is switched on rather than how it is transcribed. N-myristoylation and palmitoylation by ZDHHC21 target it to caveolae, where caveolin-1 holds it inactive until a rise in intracellular calcium loads calmodulin onto the enzyme and displaces the inhibitor; depalmitoylation reverses the lipid anchor. AKT1 phosphorylation of the reductase-domain serine raises activity and calcium sensitivity, while HSP90 acts as an activating chaperone. Cofactor and substrate supply matter as much as modification: sepiapterin reductase provides tetrahydrobiopterin, and DDAH1 degrades methylarginines that would otherwise compete with L-arginine and uncouple the enzyme toward superoxide.

Sympathetic activation shuts down insulin release so that glucose stays available during stress and exercise, and this catecholamine brake on the pancreatic beta cell is how adrenaline and noradrenaline achieve it. The signal begins at alpha-2 adrenergic receptors (ADRA2A, ADRA2C), which couple to inhibitory heterotrimeric G proteins; the released Gi alpha subunits suppress secretory granule exocytosis directly and open ATP-sensitive potassium channels to repolarize the cell, while the liberated beta-gamma dimer closes L-type voltage-gated calcium channels built from CACNA1C/CACNA1D with their auxiliary subunits and inhibits adenylyl cyclases, lowering cytosolic calcium and cAMP. The net effect opposes the glucose-triggered depolarization and calcium influx that normally drive granule fusion. Variants in ADRA2A have been linked to impaired insulin secretion and type 2 diabetes risk, and alpha-2 agonists suppress insulin output pharmacologically.

Cells must keep balanced pools of all eight ribo- and deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates for transcription, replication, repair and energy metabolism, and the interconversion of nucleotide di- and triphosphates is the step that does the balancing. Nucleoside monophosphate kinases such as the adenylate kinases, guanylate kinase, CMPK1 and thymidylate kinase add the second phosphate, drawing almost always on ATP, while the broadly specific NME family transfers the terminal phosphate to make triphosphates. Because these reactions sit near equilibrium and overlap in substrate preference, an excess of one nucleotide can be redistributed to replenish scarcer ones. Ribonucleotide reductase, with its thioredoxin and glutaredoxin reducing systems, diverts diphosphates into the deoxy series, and dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase remove species that would otherwise be misincorporated into DNA. Imbalance here causes replication stress, mutagenesis and mitochondrial DNA depletion.

Inositol pyrophosphates are high-energy signalling molecules made in the cytosol by adding further phosphates to the already fully phosphorylated inositol ring, giving diphospho- and triphosphoinositol species such as 5-IP7 and IP8. They act as metabolic and phosphate-status sensors, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, phosphate homeostasis, vesicle trafficking, telomere length and the response to DNA damage, partly by pyrophosphorylating target proteins and partly by competing with inositol phosphate binding sites on effectors such as the Akt PH domain. Inositol hexakisphosphate kinases generate IP7 from IP6, while diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases add the second pyrophosphate to make IP8; upstream, IPPK and ITPK1 supply the precursor pool. Diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases of the Nudix family reverse these reactions, so cytosolic levels reflect a continuous synthesis-degradation cycle. Loss of IP6K1 in mice impairs growth, fertility and insulin signalling.

High glucose is converted into a transcriptional signal for lipogenesis through PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of key metabolic factors, chiefly the carbohydrate response element binding protein ChREBP encoded by MLXIPL. When glucose flux raises xylulose-5-phosphate from the pentose phosphate pathway, this phosphatase activity is stimulated, and dephosphorylated ChREBP moves into the nucleus, partners with MLX, and occupies carbohydrate response elements to switch on glycolytic and fatty acid synthesis genes in liver and adipose tissue. The same phosphatase acts on the bifunctional 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, coupling the signal to glycolytic flux control. Catalytic subunits together with scaffolding and regulatory subunits assemble the holoenzyme that confers substrate specificity. This is the nutrient-sensing counterpart to insulin-driven lipogenic transcription, and its overactivity contributes to hepatic steatosis and dyslipidaemia.

Pancreatic beta cells secrete more insulin when glucose is accompanied by long-chain free fatty acids, and roughly half of that amplification runs through the fatty acid receptor FFAR1 (GPR40) rather than through intracellular fatty acid metabolism. The receptor couples to the Gq/11 family of heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits, which activate beta isoforms of phospholipase C; hydrolysis of membrane phosphoinositides yields inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, and the resulting release of calcium from intracellular stores reinforces the calcium rise that drives granule exocytosis. This lipid-sensing arm of nutrient-stimulated insulin release links circulating fat to glycemic control and has been pursued pharmacologically as a way to boost secretion only when glucose is elevated, with implications for type 2 diabetes and for how chronic lipid exposure alters beta cell function.

Complex III, the cytochrome bc1 reductase, passes electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c while pumping protons, and its assembly is the stepwise route by which that enzyme is built from a mitochondrially encoded core and ten or so nuclear-encoded subunits. Without it oxidative phosphorylation stalls at the middle of the respiratory chain, producing the infantile encephalopathy, liver failure, tubulopathy and lactic acidosis of complex III deficiency. Cytochrome b synthesis is chaperoned by dedicated factors including UQCC1-UQCC3 and LYRM7, cytochrome c1 and the peripheral subunits are added in defined order, and the Rieske protein UQCRFS1 is inserted last, requiring the AAA-ATPase BCS1L for its maturation. Because UQCRFS1 carries a [2Fe-2S] cluster, the mitochondrial iron-sulfur assembly machinery, with NFS1, ISCU, frataxin and their chaperones, feeds directly into this pathway; TTC19 acts later in turnover of cleaved Rieske fragments.

Rather than build every pyrimidine nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released when DNA and RNA are degraded and phosphorylate them back to nucleotide monophosphates, which then re-enter the interconversion routes that feed replication and repair. Pyrimidine salvage keeps nucleotide pools balanced at far lower energetic cost than de novo synthesis and is the dominant supply route in tissues with limited biosynthetic capacity, including mitochondria, where thymidine kinase 2 supplies dTMP for mitochondrial DNA; its loss causes mitochondrial DNA depletion and myopathy. Uridine-cytidine kinases act on the ribonucleosides, thymidine and deoxycytidine kinases on the deoxy forms, while phosphorylases and cytidine deaminase recycle or interconvert bases upstream. The same enzymes determine the activation and breakdown of nucleoside-analogue drugs, making this chemistry a determinant of chemotherapy and antiviral response.

Complex I, the entry point of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, oxidises NADH generated by glycolysis and the TCA cycle and uses the energy released to pump protons across the inner membrane, feeding the gradient that drives ATP synthesis. Its biogenesis is the stepwise construction of a ~45-subunit enzyme from separately made parts: seven hydrophobic core subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA and inserted into the membrane with help from OXA1L, and nuclear-encoded subunits of the NDUFA, NDUFB, NDUFS and NDUFV families imported from the cytosol. Modules for NADH oxidation, iron-sulfur electron relay and proton translocation are preassembled and then joined, with dedicated assembly factors such as NDUFAF1-8, ACAD9, ECSIT, TIMMDC1 and TMEM126B acting transiently, while NUBPL and chaperones supply the flavin and Fe-S cofactors. Defects in subunits or assembly factors cause isolated complex I deficiency, presenting as Leigh syndrome, encephalomyopathy and optic neuropathy.

Almost all of the ATP a human cell spends is made here, at the final step of oxidative phosphorylation, where the proton gradient built by the respiratory chain is cashed in for chemical energy. Protons flowing back into the mitochondrial matrix through the membrane-embedded F0 sector turn its rotor, and the rotation drives conformational cycling of the catalytic beta subunits in the F1 head, which bind ADP and phosphate, form ATP, and release it. The complex is a mosaic of nuclear-encoded subunits together with mitochondrially encoded ATP6 and ATP8, linked by central and peripheral stalks that hold the catalytic core against rotation. Because energy supply everywhere depends on this coupling, mutations in individual subunits or assembly factors cause complex V deficiency, presenting as encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy, and the same machinery can run in reverse to consume ATP when the membrane potential collapses.

De novo purine ribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthesis builds the purine nucleotides from scratch, assembling the ring stepwise on activated ribose-5-phosphate (PRPP) using nitrogen from glutamine and aspartate, carbon from glycine, bicarbonate and a folate-borne formyl group. The product, IMP, is then branched to AMP by an adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase pair, or to GMP through IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase. Cells need this route to supply DNA and RNA precursors, ATP and GTP for energy and signalling, and cofactors, so flux rises sharply in proliferating and rapidly dividing tissue; it is the reason IMP dehydrogenase inhibitors suppress lymphocyte expansion and why antifolates cripple nucleotide supply. Several steps are carried out by multifunctional enzymes that cluster into a metabolon, and inherited deficiency of adenylosuccinate lyase causes a neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and autistic features.

The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is the committed, irreversible step linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Without it, glucose-derived carbon cannot be burned aerobically, lactate accumulates, and patients present with congenital lactic acidosis, encephalopathy and Leigh-like neurodegeneration, since the brain depends heavily on glucose oxidation. The complex is built from many copies of a few subunits: the E1 heterotetramer (PDHA1 or its testis-specific counterpart PDHA2, with PDHB) performs thiamine-dependent oxidative decarboxylation, the E2 transacetylase DLAT carries the acetyl group on a lipoamide arm and transfers it to coenzyme A, and the flavoenzyme E3 (DLD) reoxidizes lipoamide while reducing NAD+. PDHX anchors E3 to the E2 core. Defects in PDHA1 and PDHX are the most frequent causes of complex deficiency, and flux through the reaction is further tuned by phosphorylation of E1.

Extracellular ATP and ADP act as signalling molecules, and the eight-member NTPDase family sets how long they persist by hydrolysing nucleoside tri- and diphosphates down to monophosphates. By clearing these agonists, phosphate bond hydrolysis by NTPDase proteins controls the stimulation of P2X and P2Y purinergic receptors and feeds substrate toward adenosine production, shaping platelet aggregation and haemostasis, inflammatory and immune responses, and neurotransmission and nervous system development. ENTPD1 on endothelium and regulatory T cells is the best-characterised plasma membrane member, alongside ENTPD2, ENTPD3 and ENTPD8; ENTPD4 and ENTPD7 face the lumen of intracellular organelles, while ENTPD5 and ENTPD6 can be shed as soluble enzymes. All are transmembrane glycoproteins whose catalytic apyrase-conserved regions require divalent magnesium or calcium and attack the terminal phosphate through an activated water molecule, with differing preferences among nucleotide substrates.

Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so the malate-aspartate shuttle moves its reducing equivalents indirectly, keeping the cytosol oxidized enough for glycolysis to continue while delivering electrons to the respiratory chain. Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate via the dicarboxylate carrier SLC25A11; inside, MDH2 regenerates NADH. Transaminases GOT1 and GOT2 interconvert aspartate and glutamate on either side, and the aspartate-glutamate carriers SLC25A12 and SLC25A13 co-import a proton, making the cycle unidirectional and driven by the proton-motive force. Glutamate carriers SLC25A18 and SLC25A22 feed the amino acid arm. Loss of any step starves the cytosol of NAD+ and limits aspartate, serine and glutamate supply; in the brain this presents as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and carrier defects also cause citrin deficiency with hyperammonaemia.

When glucose is abundant, the carbohydrate-responsive transcription factor ChREBP switches on the genes that convert surplus sugar into fat, coupling the fed state to lipogenesis in liver and adipose tissue. Dephosphorylation in response to feeding signals permits nuclear entry, where ChREBP (MLXIPL) heterodimerizes with its obligate partner MLX and occupies carbohydrate response elements in target promoters. The resulting programme includes liver pyruvate kinase, which drives glycolytic flux to pyruvate, together with ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, which supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA and elongate it into palmitate, and an acyltransferase step toward triglyceride assembly. This is the transcriptional arm of de novo lipogenesis that acts in parallel with insulin-driven SREBP signalling, and its overactivity contributes to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia, while loss impairs the storage of dietary carbohydrate as fat.

Insulin does more than push glucose into cells; it reshapes carbon flux so that glycolytic intermediates accumulate and feed the non-oxidative arm of the pentose phosphate pathway, raising cytosolic xylulose-5-phosphate. The two enzymes that carry this step, transketolase and transaldolase, interconvert fructose-6-phosphate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, ribose-5-phosphate and xylulose-5-phosphate, balancing sugar phosphates for nucleotide synthesis and NADPH-dependent biosynthesis. Xylulose-5-phosphate then acts as a signal rather than just a metabolite: it stimulates protein phosphatase 2A, which promotes formation of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, an allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase 1 and therefore of glycolytic commitment. The result is a feed-forward loop linking the fed state to glycolysis and lipogenic gene expression in liver and adipose tissue. Transketolase depends on thiamine pyrophosphate, which is why this arm falters in thiamine deficiency.

N-fatty-acyl amino acids are circulating lipid signals that raise energy expenditure, and the synthesis and breakdown of oleoyl-phenylalanine is the best-characterised example. The secreted enzyme PM20D1 works extracellularly and catalyses a reversible condensation, joining oleate to L-phenylalanine to form oleoyl-phe with release of water; hydrolysis is thermodynamically favoured, yet PM20D1 expression raises oleoyl-phe levels in serum and in culture medium. Leucine, isoleucine and other long-chain unsaturated fatty acids including arachidonate serve as less efficient substrates. The product acts on mitochondria, stimulating uncoupled respiration without requiring UCP1, with the adenine nucleotide translocases SLC25A4 and SLC25A5 implicated as targets. In mice, elevated oleoyl-phe accompanies increased energy expenditure and better glucose handling, placing this chemistry alongside brown-fat thermogenesis and making it of interest for obesity and metabolic disease.

De novo pyrimidine biosynthesis builds the uracil ring from scratch, supplying the UMP precursor from which all other pyrimidine nucleotides — CTP, UTP and the thymidine nucleotides of DNA — are derived. Proliferating cells depend on it to keep pace with replication and RNA synthesis, which is why it is a drug target in cancer, autoimmunity and antiparasitic therapy. Atoms are drawn from glutamine, bicarbonate and aspartate: a single multifunctional cytosolic protein carries out the first three steps through to dihydroorotate, the inner mitochondrial membrane enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase oxidises that intermediate while feeding electrons to the respiratory chain, and a bifunctional cytosolic enzyme joins orotate to PRPP and decarboxylates the product to UMP. This last step links pyrimidine supply to ribose-phosphate availability. Loss of the bifunctional enzyme causes hereditary orotic aciduria, with megaloblastic anaemia and orotate excretion.

Rather than build purine rings from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released by nucleic acid turnover and reattach them to ribose phosphate, an energetically cheap route that supplies much of the adenine and guanine nucleotide pool. Purine salvage matters most where de novo synthesis is weak: loss of HPRT1, which recycles hypoxanthine and guanine, causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while ADA deficiency poisons lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine metabolites and produces severe combined immunodeficiency. APRT handles adenine, nucleoside phosphorylase and deaminases feed bases back into the pool, and kinases such as ADK, DCK and DGUOK phosphorylate ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides, the last two also activating nucleoside analogue drugs. AMP deaminases and GMP reductases interconvert the adenine and guanine branches, linking salvage to purine balance and to urate production.

This is a mechanistic account of how uncoupling proteins dissipate the mitochondrial proton gradient, the basis of non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue. Rather than conducting protons directly, the carrier is proposed to work through fatty acid cycling: a protonated long-chain fatty acid flips across the inner membrane and releases its proton into the matrix, and UCP1 then transports the resulting fatty acid anion back to the cytosolic face, so that repeated rounds amount to net proton leak. The consequence is that substrate oxidation produces heat instead of ATP, a capacity recruited on cold exposure and of interest for energy balance and obesity. The related carriers UCP2 and UCP3, together with the brain and kidney homologues of this mitochondrial carrier family, are expressed far more widely and are linked to control of reactive oxygen species and fatty acid handling rather than thermogenesis proper.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is the committed step that converts glycolytic pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, and its regulation decides whether a cell burns glucose or conserves it. Switching the complex off spares glucose during fasting and shifts tissues onto fat oxidation; keeping it on allows glucose carbon to feed the TCA cycle for ATP and to supply acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. Control is by reversible phosphorylation of the E1 alpha subunit: four kinases (PDK1-4) inactivate the complex in response to hormonal and nutritional state, while two magnesium-dependent phosphatases (PDP1, PDP2, with the regulatory subunit PDPR) reactivate it. SIRT4 further restrains activity. Loss-of-function mutations in the core subunits cause pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency with lactic acidosis and neurological disease, and persistent PDK activity underlies the glycolytic metabolism of many tumours.

Highly phosphorylated inositols act as diffusible signals and phosphate donors inside the nucleus, where they influence chromatin regulation, mRNA export and transcription, so the cell must move inositol hexakisphosphate and the pyrophosphorylated form IP7 between cytosol and nucleus rather than making them only where they are used. This passage across the nuclear envelope is attributed to the nuclear pore complex, and the components here are its parts: the structural Y-complex scaffold with NUP107, NUP133, NUP85, SEC13 and SEH1L, the transmembrane ring anchors NDC1 and the POM121 proteins, the phenylalanine-glycine channel nucleoporins NUP62, NUP54 and NUP98 that form the permeability barrier, and peripheral elements such as NUP153, NUP50, RANBP2 and TPR on the cytoplasmic filaments and nuclear basket. How these small, densely charged metabolites are selected and translocated is not established, so the pathway is best read as the conduit rather than a defined carrier mechanism.

2-Hydroxyglutarate is a metabolic dead end that cells must clear, and this small mitochondrial route returns both of its stereoisomers to 2-oxoglutarate so the carbon can enter the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases do the oxidation with opposite stereospecificity: D2HGDH acts on the R(-) isomer and L2HGDH on the S(-) isomer. ADHFE1 provides a separate, reversible link, transferring reducing equivalents between R(-)-2-hydroxyglutarate and succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate, tying this chemistry to GABA-related metabolism. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase causes D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with accumulation of the acid and variable encephalopathy, seizures and developmental delay. The interest in these reactions is broader than the rare diseases, since 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases that control DNA and histone demethylation.

Inositol phosphates are small, highly charged signalling molecules, and several of the kinases that make them work in the nucleus, so the products must reach the cytosol to act on calcium release, phosphate sensing, vesicle traffic and other targets. This step describes that movement of inositol phosphates between nucleus and cytosol, which keeps nuclear synthesis coupled to cytoplasmic signalling; the transport mechanism itself is not well defined. The proteins assigned to it are the constituents of the nuclear pore complex: the scaffold Y-complex members such as NUP107, NUP133 and SEC13, transmembrane anchors including NDC1 and POM121, the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins NUP62 and NUP98 that form the permeability barrier, and the basket components TPR and NUP153. Passage of a small metabolite through this aqueous channel is therefore treated as diffusion across the pore rather than carrier-mediated transport.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase must sit at the right membrane to make the nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and NOSTRIN-mediated eNOS trafficking is how endothelial cells pull it away from that site. NOSTRIN binds eNOS and moves it from the plasma membrane into intracellular vesicular compartments, lowering nitric oxide output; because endothelium-derived nitric oxide controls vessel tone, platelet adhesion and permeability, this relocalisation is a way of tuning vascular relaxation, and its dysregulation belongs to the broader picture of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and atherosclerosis. Mechanistically NOSTRIN trimerises and uses its SH3 domain as an adaptor, gathering eNOS together with dynamin-2 and the N-WASP homologue encoded by WASL; dynamin drives vesicle fission while N-WASP recruits the Arp2/3 complex to nucleate actin. Caveolin-1 places the process in caveolae, linking nitric oxide signalling to caveolar endocytosis and actin remodelling.

Higher inositol phosphates are best known as cytosolic signalling and phosphate-storage molecules, but a branch of their metabolism runs inside the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, where inositol polyphosphates are trimmed rather than built up. This compartmentalised turnover is carried out by multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase MINPP1, a broadly acting histidine phosphatase that removes phosphate groups from IP4, IP5 and IP6 to generate lower inositol phosphate species. Because the enzyme is separated from the cytosolic kinases that generate its substrates, its activity is thought to shape the pool of inositol phosphates available when membrane integrity is lost or substrates enter the secretory pathway, with consequences for calcium signalling and phosphate handling. Loss of MINPP1 function in humans causes a severe pontocerebellar hypoplasia, linking this lumenal dephosphorylation step to brain development.

Nudix hydrolases keep the cellular nucleotide pool clean, and the phosphate bond hydrolysis they carry out is best understood as sanitation: damaged or surplus nucleotides are cleaved before they can be used as substrates. Oxidised, deaminated or methylated purine nucleoside di- and triphosphates are degraded by enzymes such as NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, preventing their incorporation into DNA as mutations or into mRNA as mistranslated protein. NUDT16 acts on inosine- and other modified guanine-containing nucleotides, while NUDT9 and NUDT5 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, limiting non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and the accumulation of a potent second messenger; ADPRM degrades ADP-ribose 1''-phosphate from tRNA splicing. Because these enzymes also destroy nucleotide analogues, their activity sets tolerance to thiopurine and other nucleoside-based chemotherapies, and NUDT15 variants cause severe drug toxicity.

The incretin effect — why an oral glucose load releases far more insulin than the same glucose given intravenously — rests on this signalling route, in which intestinal L-cell-derived GLP-1 amplifies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. It is the target of the GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors used in type 2 diabetes, and its potentiation of secretion is glucose-dependent, so it raises insulin output without provoking hypoglycaemia. GLP-1 binding to its Gs-coupled receptor frees the Gs alpha subunit to stimulate adenylate cyclases, and the resulting cAMP acts through two effectors: protein kinase A, whose catalytic subunits are released from regulatory subunits and organised by anchoring proteins, and the exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2, which load GTP onto Rap1A. Downstream, potassium channel closure, IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum, and granule priming drive exocytosis, while transcriptional effects support beta cell mass.

Cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the respiratory chain, transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen and pumps protons; complex IV assembly is the stepwise construction of this enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It matters because the mature complex requires far more proteins than it contains: three mitochondrially encoded core subunits, eleven nuclear-encoded subunits, and a large set of factors that insert heme a, the CuA and CuB copper centres, and bound phospholipids. Copper delivery runs through soluble and membrane metallochaperones such as COX17, SCO1 and SCO2, while COX15 supplies heme a and translational activators like TACO1 ensure core subunit synthesis. Subunit paralogues and hypoxia-responsive members permit tissue- and oxygen-tuned versions of the enzyme, and some factors also govern supercomplex formation. Loss of any subunit or assembly factor produces cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, typically presenting as Leigh syndrome and other infantile encephalomyopathies.

When cellular ATP falls, AMP-activated protein kinase shuts down anabolic spending, and one of its targets is the glucose-responsive transcription factor ChREBP. Phosphorylation of ChREBP blocks its ability to occupy carbohydrate response elements, so transcription of glycolytic and lipogenic enzymes drops and the liver stops converting sugar into fat while energy is scarce. The arrangement links nutrient sensing to lipid synthesis: the AMPK heterotrimer of catalytic, beta and gamma subunits is switched on by the upstream kinase LKB1 when the AMP:ATP ratio rises, and adiponectin acting through its receptors ADIPOR1 and ADIPOR2 provides a hormonal route to the same kinase. Loss of this restraint contributes to hepatic steatosis and the dyslipidaemia of insulin resistance, which is why adiponectin signalling and AMPK activation are pursued as metabolic drug targets.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase must sit in plasma membrane caveolae to make nitric oxide efficiently, and NOSIP-mediated trafficking is one way that localisation is taken away from it. By binding the carboxy-terminal region of the eNOS oxygenase domain, this nucleocytoplasmic shuttling protein pulls the enzyme off caveolae and onto the cytoskeleton, where its output of nitric oxide falls. The consequence is felt in the vasculature: nitric oxide from endothelium relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelet aggregation and limits leukocyte adhesion, so relocalising its source is a way to tune vascular tone and blood pressure without changing how much enzyme is present. Because NOSIP accumulates in the cytoplasm during G2, this represents a point where cell cycle position feeds into endothelial signalling output, and it illustrates control of an enzyme by compartment rather than by transcription.

The alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex carries out one of the rate-limiting steps of the citric acid cycle, converting 2-oxoglutarate, coenzyme A and NAD+ into succinyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. Because it sits at the branch point where carbon leaving the cycle feeds glutamate and amino acid metabolism, its flux sets how much reducing power reaches the respiratory chain and how much nitrogen handling the mitochondrion can support. The complex is a large assembly: a core of DLST subunits bearing lipoamide arms, decorated with OGDH dimers that decarboxylate the substrate, DLD dimers that reoxidise dihydrolipoamide and pass electrons to NAD+, and an accessory subunit (KGD4/MRPS36) that stabilises E3 binding. It is also a notable source of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and loss of DLD or DLST activity produces encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and tumour-associated metabolite accumulation.

Inositol phosphates are not confined to membranes; a soluble, highly phosphorylated series is built inside the nucleus, and these molecules act as diffusible signals and phosphate donors rather than as lipid second messengers. Their production couples cellular phosphate and energy status to chromatin and RNA metabolism, with roles in mRNA export, transcriptional control, DNA repair and apoptosis, and it shapes how cells sense and store phosphate. In this nuclear branch, a multikinase phosphorylates lower inositol phosphates to IP4 and IP5, a 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add a high-energy pyrophosphate to generate IP7 and IP8, which can transfer phosphate to target proteins. Loss of individual kinases alters growth signalling and stress responses, and the same enzymes influence insulin secretion and tumour cell survival, placing nuclear inositol polyphosphate synthesis upstream of both gene expression and metabolic regulation.

Receptor-driven calcium signalling begins when phospholipase C cleaves membrane PIP2 to release inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, and the cytosolic inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases collected here decide how long that signal lasts and what it becomes. The many PLC isoforms differ in how they are switched on al by G protein-coupled receptors, by tyrosine kinase receptors through PLCG1 and PLCG2, or by calcium itself al so the same second messenger reports on very different stimuli. Inositol trisphosphate 3-kinases such as ITPKA and ITPKB convert IP3 into inositol tetrakisphosphate, while 5-phosphatases including OCRL, INPPL1, INPP5D and synaptojanin strip phosphates and terminate signalling. The resulting pool of IP3 and IP4 species controls store release of calcium, membrane trafficking and lipid identity; loss of OCRL causes Lowe syndrome, and INPP5D shapes immune receptor thresholds.

Free myo-inositol is the starting material for all inositol lipids and inositol phosphates, and the cytosolic steps that generate IP2, IP and inositol are how cells recover it after receptor-stimulated phospholipase C signalling. A cascade of position-specific phosphatases strips phosphates from higher inositol phosphates and from lipid-derived species, ending with inositol monophosphatases that release free inositol; inositol-3-phosphate synthase provides a de novo route from glucose 6-phosphate, and an oxygenase route feeds inositol catabolism. The activity matters because it terminates calcium-mobilising and PI3K-derived signals while replenishing substrate for PIP2 resynthesis. Several members are disease genes: loss of the 5-phosphatase OCRL causes Lowy oculocerebrorenal syndrome, synaptojanin supports clathrin-mediated synaptic vesicle recycling, and INPP4B acts as a tumour suppressor. Lithium's inhibition of inositol monophosphatases places this recycling route in mood-disorder pharmacology.

Pancreatic beta cells amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release when fatty acids are available, and part of that amplification comes from burning the fatty acids rather than from surface receptor signalling. Long-chain fatty acids enter through the scavenger receptor CD36, are activated to their coenzyme A thioesters by acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL3 and ACSL4, and the resulting acyl-CoAs can be carried into mitochondria for beta oxidation. The ATP generated raises the cytosolic ATP:ADP ratio, closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, depolarising the membrane and opening voltage-gated calcium channels so that insulin granules fuse. This nutrient-sensing arithmetic links circulating lipid supply to insulin output; chronic fatty acid excess distorts it, contributing to beta cell lipotoxicity and the secretory failure of type 2 diabetes. The same enzymes operate throughout the body, but their combination and localisation here tie lipid catabolism directly to hormone secretion.

The citric acid cycle enzymes do not work as made: several require cofactor insertion, assembly factors, or covalent modification before they can turn, and this maturation and regulatory layer sets how much flux the cycle can carry. Aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase both depend on iron-sulfur clusters built by the mitochondrial scaffold machinery, with a cysteine desulfurase, frataxin, and the ISCU/ISCA carriers supplying and transferring the clusters; succinate dehydrogenase additionally needs dedicated SDHAF chaperones for flavinylation and for loading its iron-sulfur subunit into the membrane complex. Citrate synthase is trimethylated on a single lysine by CSKMT, a modification opposed by oxaloacetate, and the deacetylase SIRT3 tunes several of these enzymes according to nutrient state. Loss of individual factors causes mitochondrial disease, paraganglioma, or Friedreich ataxia, placing this step upstream of oxidative energy metabolism rather than within it.

When hormones such as glucagon or adrenaline raise cAMP, protein kinase A tetramers dissociate and the freed catalytic subunits phosphorylate enzymes that set the direction of glucose metabolism. This is the switch that turns a fed, glucose-storing liver or muscle cell into one that mobilises glycogen and exports glucose, and its loss would leave tissues unable to respond to fasting or stress. Phosphorylation of the bifunctional 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, relieving stimulation of glycolysis and favouring gluconeogenesis, while parallel targeting of glycogen synthase and the phosphorylase activation cascade shifts glycogen handling toward breakdown. The kinase also phosphorylates the carbohydrate-responsive transcription factor ChREBP, keeping it out of the nucleus and shutting down transcription of glycolytic and lipogenic genes. Three catalytic subunit isoforms provide the enzymatic activity, linking G protein-coupled receptor signalling to both acute enzyme control and longer-term metabolic gene expression.

Pyrimidine catabolism disposes of uracil and thymine released from nucleotide turnover and dietary nucleic acids, converting them in three steps each to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, which are excreted in urine or transaminated further. Upstream, nucleotidases such as NT5E and NT5C dephosphorylate pyrimidine monophosphates and phosphorylases including UPP1 and thymidine phosphorylase remove the sugar, feeding free bases into the degradative arm. There dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase reduces the ring, dihydropyrimidinase opens it, and beta-ureidopropionase releases the final amino acid with ammonia and CO2. The route matters clinically because it is the same one that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: DPYD deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal 5-fluorouracil toxicity, and inherited defects at each step produce neurological disease with pyrimidine accumulation. Mitochondrial AGXT2 can divert the end products toward branched-chain amino acid and short-chain fatty acid metabolism.

When blood glucose falls, glucagon acts on hepatocytes to mobilise stored fuel, and this step is where the hormonal signal becomes an intracellular one. The stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS switches on membrane adenylate cyclases, which convert ATP into cyclic AMP. Protein kinase A rests as a tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, the complex dissociates, and free catalytic monomers phosphorylate targets that drive glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression and lipolysis. Several adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms exist with distinct tissue distributions and cAMP sensitivities, tuning the amplitude of the response. Loss or gain of function in this cascade disturbs glucose homeostasis, and activating GNAS mutations or regulatory subunit loss cause endocrine tumour syndromes, underscoring that cAMP output must be held within narrow limits.
